questions.question: Will Argentina's economy grow at 3.5% or faster in 2026?
questions.resolution_criteria: Resolves to the outcome of the question found at https://www.metaculus.com/questions/44529.
questions.background:
*This forecasting question is associated with the Verity controversy:* [*Will Argentina's economy grow at 3.5% or faster in 2026?*](https://www.verity.news/controversy/will-argentinas-economy-grow-at-35-or-faster-in-2026)

Argentina has experienced repeated cycles of recession, high inflation, sovereign debt crises, and currency instability over the past two decades. [The country defaulted on its sovereign debt in 2001 and again restructured its debt in later years](https://debtjustice.org.uk/countries/argentina), while persistent fiscal deficits, capital controls, and chronic inflation constrained long-term growth. [By 2023, annual inflation had exceeded 200%](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/oecd-economic-surveys-argentina-2025_27dd6e27-en/full-report/macroeconomic-developments-and-policy-challenges_8e6a0236.html), foreign exchange reserves were severely depleted, and the economy had entered another recession, highlighting longstanding structural weaknesses in public finances and monetary policy.

Following the [election of President Javier Milei in late 2023](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Argentine_general_election#:~:text=In%20the%20run%2Doff%2C%20Milei,vote%20total%20in%20Argentina's%20history.), Argentina implemented an ambitious economic stabilization program [centered on fiscal austerity, deregulation, reductions in public spending, and market-oriented reforms](https://www.spglobal.com/ratings/en/regulatory/article/credit-faq-this-time-could-be-different-for-argentina-s101690623). The government achieved its [first sustained fiscal surpluses in years, sharply reduced monetary financing of deficits, and gradually eased many exchange-rate and capital controls.](https://ca.finance.yahoo.com/news/argentinas-challenge-making-economic-reform-130007407.html) While these measures initially deepened the recession, inflation slowed significantly and investor confidence improved, with [support from a new IMF program and from other international financial institutions.](https://www.reuters.com/world/americas/imf-confident-argentina-repayment-even-after-staff-flags-exceptional-risks-2026-06-25/)

Economic activity rebounded during 2025 as agriculture recovered from earlier droughts, energy production expanded—particularly from the [Vaca Muerta shale formation](https://oilprice.com/Energy/Energy-General/Argentinas-Vaca-Muerta-Shale-Is-Smashing-Oil-Production-Records-in-2025.html)—and investment strengthened under new incentives for large-scale projects. Nevertheless, [domestic demand remained constrained by high real interest rates, declining purchasing power, and the ongoing adjustment process](https://www.vizionapi.com/blog/argentinas-economic-transformation-under-javier-milei-from-crisis-to-opportunity). Growth increasingly relied on export-oriented sectors such as agriculture, mining, and energy, while inflation, though much lower than its 2023 peak, remained elevated by international standards.

Whether Argentina's economy grows by at least 3.5% in 2026 will depend on the durability of the stabilization program and the strength of the recovery. [Major forecasters have projected continued expansion, but estimates differ.](https://www.bbvaresearch.com/en/publicaciones/argentina-economic-outlook-june-2026/) The [IMF projects real GDP growth of approximately 3.5% in 2026](https://www.imf.org/en/countries/arg), while the [World Bank projects 3.6%,](https://www.worldbank.org/ext/en/country/argentina#tab-economy) reflecting optimism about investment and export growth. The [OECD is somewhat more cautious, forecasting growth below 3.5%](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/oecd-economic-outlook-volume-2026-issue-1_2d1956f0-en/full-report/argentina_0e535e2a.html), citing weaker household consumption and lingering macroeconomic vulnerabilities. As a result, the 3.5% threshold sits close to the middle of current consensus forecasts, making continued reform implementation, inflation reduction, financing conditions, and commodity export performance key factors for the outcome.

The First Trump Administration saw a pattern of withdrawing from international arms control agreements, including:

* **INF Treaty (**[**2019**](https://www.defense.gov/News/News-Stories/article/article/1924779/us-withdraws-from-intermediate-range-nuclear-forces-treaty/)**)** – U.S. withdrawal from the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty with Russia.
* **Open Skies Treaty (**[**2020**](https://www.armscontrol.org/act/2020-12/news/us-completes-open-skies-treaty-withdrawal)**)** – Trump announced withdrawal, citing Russian non-compliance.
* **Iran Nuclear Deal (**[**2018**](https://www.nytimes.com/2018/05/08/world/middleeast/trump-iran-nuclear-deal.html)**)** – The U.S. exited the JCPOA, leading to renewed tensions.

With Trump's return to office in 2025, attention has turned to whether his administration might again seek to exit existing arms control agreements. The agreements most at risk include:

1. [**New START**](https://www.state.gov/new-start-treaty) **(Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty)**, the last remaining U.S.-Russia nuclear arms control treaty, limiting strategic nuclear warheads and delivery systems. It is set to expire in February 2026, but there are concerns that Trump may refuse renewal or suspend compliance before then.
2. [**The Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC)**](https://www.opcw.org/chemical-weapons-convention), a global ban on chemical weapons with strong bipartisan support, but potential friction due to compliance disputes with China and Russia.
3. [**The Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT)**](https://disarmament.unoda.org/wmd/nuclear/npt/), the cornerstone of global nuclear non-proliferation. While withdrawal is unlikely, Trump has expressed skepticism toward arms control constraints in the past.
4. [**The Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty (CTBT)**](https://www.ctbto.org/our-mission/the-treaty), though never ratified by the U.S., Trump officials previously floated the idea of resuming nuclear testing.
questions.market_info_resolution_criteria:
This question will resolve as Yes if, before January 1, 2027, credible sources report that the Trump administration has formally attempted to withdraw from or suspend U.S. participation in at least one of the following seven international arms control agreements:

* New START (Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty)
* The Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC)
* The Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT)
* The Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty (CTBT)
* Biological Weapons Convention (BWC)
* Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW)
* Outer Space Treaty (OST)

A formal initiation of withdrawal is defined as one or more of the following actions:

* An official written notification of withdrawal or intent to withdraw sent to treaty depositaries, treaty partners, or relevant international bodies (eg. the UN).
* A public executive action or directive explicitly stating that the United States is withdrawing from the treaty.
* A formal declaration of suspension or non-compliance that is explicitly framed by the administration as terminating U.S. participation in the treaty.

questions.question: Will the Brookmont Catastrophic Bond ETF drop at least $0.25 within two days before September 2026?
questions.resolution_criteria: Resolves to the outcome of the question found at https://www.metaculus.com/questions/43824.
questions.background:
Catastrophe bonds are insurance-linked securities that let insurers and reinsurers transfer the risk of natural disasters to capital-market investors. In calm periods investors collect an attractive yield; on the other hand, they can lose principal if a covered event (generally a hurricane, flood, earthquake, or wildfire) breaches the bond's predefined trigger.

The [Brookmont Catastrophic Bond ETF](https://ilsetf.com/ils) (NYSEARCA: ILS), launched in April 2025 as the first US-listed catastrophe bond ETF, holds a diversified portfolio of [roughly 102 such bonds](https://seekingalpha.com/article/4910536-ils-year-of-existence-revisiting-this-catastrophe-bond-fund-downgrade), heavily weighted toward US exposure. ILS is actively managed and its holdings may change at the discretion of its managers. ILS has little sensitivity to interest-rate fluctuations as its yield is floating-rate.

ILS trades near \$20 and has been remarkably stable, with its entire 52-week range spanning under a dollar. A drop of \$0.25 (about 1.25%) would therefore be an outsized move for this fund, most plausibly driven by a major catastrophe forcing markdowns across exposed holdings or by a broad repricing of catastrophe bond risk. A decline of that size would imply a disaster severe enough to threaten billions in insured losses, on the scale that has historically dented the entire catastrophe bond market.

The window of this question coincides with peak danger months: the Atlantic hurricane season began June 1 and runs into November, while Western US wildfire activity typically intensifies through summer and early fall.
questions.market_info_resolution_criteria: This question will resolve as **Yes** if, on any trading day after June 15, 2026 and before September 1, 2026, the Adjusted Close price of the Brookmont Catastrophic Bond ETF (NYSEARCA: ILS), as reported by [Yahoo Finance](https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/ILS/), is at least \$0.25 lower than its Adjusted Close on the most recent trading day at least two calendar days earlier.

questions.question: Will Sudan's Emergency Response Rooms win the Nobel Peace Prize in 2026?
questions.resolution_criteria: Resolves to the outcome of the question found at https://www.metaculus.com/questions/41804.
questions.background:
Sudan's Emergency Response Rooms (ERRs) are a decentralized network of over 735 volunteer-run neighborhood rooms across Sudan's 18 states. Emerging from the 2019 revolution's resistance committees, they have provided food, shelter, medical evacuations, and emergency response to more than 11.5 million people with nearly 26,000 volunteers since civil war erupted in April 2023, per the Right Livelihood Award and Rafto Foundation announcements in late 2024.

In 2025, ERRs were front-runners for the Nobel Peace Prize. They ranked first on the [PRIO Director's shortlist](https://www.prio.org/news/3596), which has correctly identified the winner in 10 of 12 years since 2014. On [Polymarket](https://polymarket.com/event/nobel-peace-prize-winner-2025/will-sudans-emergency-response-rooms-win-the-nobel-peace-prize-in-2025), ERRs reached 33% odds by October 9, 2025, the highest among candidates. The prize went to Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado.

The same year, ERRs received the [Rafto Prize for Human Rights](https://www.rafto.no/en/the-rafto-prize/emergency-response-rooms-of-sudan-err) and the [Right Livelihood Award](https://rightlivelihood.org/the-change-makers/find-a-laureate/emergency-response-rooms/), both sometimes called "alternative Nobels." Four Rafto Prize winners have later won the Nobel Peace Prize: Aung San Suu Kyi (Rafto 1990, Nobel 1991), Kim Dae-jung (Rafto 2000, Nobel 2000), Shirin Ebadi (Rafto 2001, Nobel 2003), and Jose Ramos-Horta.

As of January 22nd 2026, ERRs do not appear on the [2026 Polymarket Nobel Peace Prize market](https://polymarket.com/event/nobel-peace-prize-winner-2026-139).
questions.market_info_resolution_criteria:
This question resolves YES if the Norwegian Nobel Committee announces the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize to include Sudan's Emergency Response Rooms (ERRs), as published on [nobelprize.org](nobelprize.org).

The prize may be shared with other laureates. The question resolves Yes if ERRs are among the named recipients.

This question resolves NO if the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize is awarded to any individual or organization that does not include the ERRs.

questions.background:
[ElevenLabs](https://elevenlabs.io/) je firmou z oblasti generativní AI zaměřená na syntézu hlasu (text-to-speech), *voice cloning* a tvorbu audio nástrojů pro tvůrce i firmy. Její hlavní službou je nabídka API a aplikace, díky kterým lze generovat přirozeně znějící řeč v mnoha jazycích a stylech, případně vytvářet hlasové modely (např. pro dabing, audioknihy, zákaznické linky, hlasové asistenty a „AI agenty“). Společnost byla založena v roce 2022 a rychle získala pozornost kvalitou výstupu a jednoduchou integrací pro vývojáře i mediální domy. Mezi uživatele patří i řada zaměstnanců Fortune 500 firem.

Po startu v roce 2023 následoval rychlý fundraising a skoky ve valuacích. V lednu 2024 se v médiích psalo o [Series B](https://elevenlabs.io/blog/series-b) (80 mil. USD) a valuaci kolem 1,1 mld. USD. V lednu 2025 firma oznámila [Series C](https://elevenlabs.io/blog/series-c) (180 mil. USD) při valuaci 3,3 mld. USD. V září 2025 pak proběhl zaměstnanecký sekundární prodej/tender při valuaci 6,6 mld. USD. Reuters u toho zároveň popsal výrazný růst ARR (řádově stovky milionů USD) a rychlý nábor personálu, což jsou typické signály, které trh používá k ospravedlnění vyšších valuací, zároveň jde o sektor se silnou konkurencí a regulatorními/reputačními riziky (zneužití hlasových deepfaků, autentizace, souhlasy a práva k hlasu). Podle investorů, se kterými jsme pro tuto výzvu v kontaktu, už nyní přesahuje hodnota ElevenLabs 10 mld. USD.

Jeho plán je ambiciózní - nejen chyby najít, ale automaticky vytvářet opravy (např. patch/pull request), ověřovat je a eliminovat backlog zranitelností. Podle [odborníků](https://www.edgescan.com/the-vulnerability-backlog-crisis-why-45-of-enterprise-vulnerabilities-never-get-fixed/) na kyberbezpečnost organizace běžně žijí se tisíci až miliony nevyřešenými zranitelnostmi a že opravy často trvají týdny až měsíce – což AISLE plánuje zásadně zkrátit. 

Fortune 500 zákazníci jsou pro podobný produkt klíčovým zákazníkem a zároveň testem. Obvykle mají rozsáhlé služby, složitou a rozsáhlou infrastrukturu, náročné compliance postupy, a zároveň prostředky na špičková řešení. questions.question: Will any U.S. state or EU member state restrict large-scale data center grid connections before September 2026?
questions.resolution_criteria: Resolves to the outcome of the question found at https://www.metaculus.com/questions/43494.
questions.background:
The rapid expansion of AI infrastructure has placed unprecedented pressure on electricity grids across the United States and Europe. The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) [projected in January 2026](https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/steo/archives/Jan26.pdf) that electricity demand growth will accelerate significantly, with large computing facilities identified as a primary driver. The U.S. Department of Energy has [similarly identified data centers](https://www.energy.gov/oe/clean-energy-resources-meet-data-center-electricity-demand) as a critical short-term demand factor.

In Europe, grid connection queues [have reached record lengths](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/05/04/denmark-data-centers-moratorium-grid-pause-power-demand.html) in Ireland, the Netherlands, and Denmark — jurisdictions that have previously imposed informal or formal restrictions on new data center connections. Ireland's EirGrid and the Dutch transmission operator TenneT have both taken administrative action to limit new connections in recent years, establishing a precedent base rate for this type of regulatory action.

As of May 2026, several U.S. states including Virginia, Texas, and Georgia — home to the [largest data center concentrations](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2026/04/13/most-new-data-centers-in-the-us-are-coming-to-rural-areas/) in the country — are actively reviewing grid capacity allocation for high-load facilities.
questions.market_info_resolution_criteria:
This question will resolve as **Yes** if, at any point before September 1, 2026, either a U.S. state or an EU member state announces a new moratorium, suspension, or binding restrictive rule applying to new grid connection requests from large-scale data centers, and the restriction is not officially reversed or rescinded before September 1, 2026, according to [credible sources](https://www.metaculus.com/faq/#definitions).

Large-scale datacenters are defined as facilities with contracted or requested grid capacity of 50 MW or more.

questions.question: Will federal courts block the USPS mail-in ballot restrictions before Election Day?
questions.resolution_criteria: Resolves to the outcome of the question found at https://www.metaculus.com/questions/43527.
questions.background:
Mail-in voting, also known as postal voting, has a long history [in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postal_voting_in_the_United_States), though it has increased in popularity and salience since the coronavirus pandemic prompted [many more Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postal_voting_in_the_2020_United_States_elections) to vote by mail in 2020. At the same time, U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly and for years [expressed concern](https://www.npr.org/2020/08/19/903886567/trump-while-attacking-mail-voting-casts-mail-ballot-again) about mail-in voting, suggesting that it creates too great an opportunity for election fraud.

Every American state offers at least some form of mail-in voting: In many states, voters may choose to vote by mail for any reason at all. In some other states, voters may vote by mail only if they have a [statutorily approved reason](https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/table-2-excuses-to-vote-absentee) (for example, because they will be traveling on Election Day, because they are unwell or disabled, or even simply because they are aged). Finally, in still other states, elections are held entirely via mail, and all eligible voters receive a mail-in ballot without needing to request one.

Nevertheless, on March 31, 2026, President Trump issued [an executive order](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2026/03/ensuring-citizenship-verification-and-integrity-in-federal-elections/) calling on the Postmaster General to issue regulations requiring individuals to enroll with the United States Postal Service in order to be eligible to transmit a ballot through the mail. The executive order also calls on the Secretary of Homeland Security to assemble lists of U.S. citizens age 18 and order in each state and to send those lists to each state's election officials.

This executive action was immediately challenged in federal court. On April 1, 2026, various organs of the Democratic Party [filed suit](https://www.democracydocket.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/1-2026-04-01-Complaint-2.pdf) in federal district court in Washington, D.C. On April 2, the League of Women Voters (LWV) and other organizations [filed suit](https://www.democracydocket.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/2026-04-02-Complaint.pdf) in federal district court in Massachusetts, and the League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC) and other organizations [filed suit](https://www.democracydocket.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/2026-04-02-Complaint-1.pdf) in D.C. federal court. On April 3, [various blue states](https://www.democracydocket.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/2026-04-03-Complaint-1.pdf) also filed suit in Massachusetts, and [the NAACP and other organizations](https://www.democracydocket.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/gov.uscourts.dcd_.291146.1.0DD.pdf) also filed suit in D.C.

The three lawsuits filed in D.C. were consolidated, and a group of red states were allowed to intervene as additional defendants. The consolidated cases are currently being heard by [Judge Carl Nichols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_J._Nichols), a Trump appointee. On May 28, 2026, Judge Nichols [denied plaintiffs' request for a preliminary injunction](https://fingfx.thomsonreuters.com/gfx/legaldocs/zdvxgzbdnpx/DCD%20-%20Mail-in%20ballot%20ruling%2020260528.pdf), stating that until the Postal Service took further action, the plaintiffs' claims were not ripe.

The two lawsuits filed in Massachusetts are both before [Judge Indira Talwani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Talwani), an appointee of President Barack Obama, who has refused to transfer the cases to the D.C. court. The two lawsuits have been partially consolidated, and Judge Talwani has allowed the group of red states to intervene in the LWV's suit but not in the suit brought by blue states (though the red states are currently appealing that latter decision). Judge Talwani is scheduled to hear arguments on the LWV plaintiffs' request for a preliminary injunction and the blue states' request for a permanent injunction on June 2, 2026.

Decisions granting or denying injunctions [may be appealed immediately](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/28/1292).
questions.market_info_resolution_criteria: This question will resolve as **Yes** if, on Election Day (November 3, 2026), a federal court order (e.g., injunction, stay, or vacatur) is in effect that prevents the federal government from restricting which voters' mail-in or absentee ballots the United States Postal Service will transmit for the 2026 general election.

VDH tracks the number of [new COVID-19 cases](https://www.vdh.virginia.gov/coronavirus/see-the-numbers/covid-19-in-virginia/covid-19-in-virginia-cases/) by date of symptom onset, which it [currently](https://www.vdh.virginia.gov/coronavirus/see-the-numbers/dashboardschedule/)  updates on weekdays.

These data may not represent confirmed cases of COVID-19, but they can assist with understanding the burden on healthcare systems and the community.”

questions.question: Will a public, formal bilateral military agreement between Turkey and the Syrian government explicitly allowing Turkish troops to be stationed south of Aleppo be signed before 31 December 2026?
questions.resolution_criteria: Resolves to the outcome of the question found at https://www.randforecastinginitiative.org/questions/1773.
questions.background:
Since the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024, Turkey and Syria's transitional government under President Ahmed al-Sharaa have rapidly deepened military ties. In February 2025, al-Sharaa visited Ankara, where the two sides announced plans to elevate their relationship to a "strategic level" and began negotiating a joint defense pact (Breaking Defense). On 13 August 2025, Turkish Defense Minister Yasar Guler and his Syrian counterpart Murhaf Abu Qasra signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) on military training and consultancy, under which Turkey pledged to provide weapons systems, logistical support, and training to the Syrian army (Euronews). However, that MoU explicitly stopped short of authorizing the deployment of Turkish troops to bases inside Syria (Middle East Eye).

A broader defense pact that would establish Turkish military bases in central Syria–including at the T4 airbase near Palmyra in Homs province and the Palmyra military airport, both well south of Aleppo–has been under negotiation since at least December 2024 but remains unsigned as of question writing (Middle East Eye). Israeli airstrikes on the proposed base sites in March and April 2025, as well as broader Israeli opposition to expanded Turkish military presence, have complicated the talks (Jerusalem Post). Turkey already maintains military positions within formerly Syrian National Army-controlled territory in northern Syria, and in October 2025 Turkey's parliament extended its mandate for cross-border military operations in Syria and Iraq by three years (Nordic Monitor). In February, Turkey's defense minister stated that Ankara has "no agenda for withdrawing" from Syria (P.A. Turkey).

 

Resolution Criteria: 

This question will be resolved using official statements, press releases, or documents published by the Turkish Ministry of National Defense, the Syrian Ministry of Defense, or the official websites or social media accounts of the Turkish or Syrian governments. As a secondary source, credible reporting by major international or regional media outlets (e.g., Reuters, Associated Press, Al Jazeera, Middle East Eye, Anadolu Agency) citing official confirmation from both parties may be used.

This question resolves “Yes” if, before the end date, Turkey and the Syrian government sign a public, formal bilateral military agreement (such as a defense pact, treaty, memorandum of understanding, or similar instrument) that explicitly authorizes the stationing or deployment of Turkish military personnel at one or more locations in an area that includes territory south of the city of Aleppo, whether or not specific locations are named in the agreement.

For purposes of this question, 'troops' refers to military personnel deployed in a stationing, basing, or garrison capacity, regardless of the label used in the agreement. Personnel operating solely as advisors or trainers under the existing August 2025 MoU do not qualify.

The agreement must be officially acknowledged by at least one of the Turkish and Syrian governments through government statements, press releases, official websites, or credible reporting by reputable international or regional media outlets citing official confirmation from both sides.

The following will NOT be sufficient for resolution:

  • Extensions, amendments, or implementation of the existing 13 August 2025 training and consultancy MoU, unless a new or amended agreement explicitly adds provisions authorizing the stationing of Turkish troops south of Aleppo
  • Informal or undisclosed arrangements reported solely by anonymous sources without official confirmation from both governments
  • The continued presence of Turkish military personnel in northern Aleppo Governorate or areas north of the city of Aleppo under existing deployments
  • Unilateral Turkish military operations conducted without a bilateral agreement with the Syrian government

questions.question: Will the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) signatories publicly announce the establishment of a formal coordinating body by 31 December 2026?
questions.resolution_criteria: Resolves to the outcome of the question found at https://www.randforecastinginitiative.org/questions/1761.
questions.background:
The India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) is a planned multimodal transport and infrastructure corridor linking India, the Middle East, and Europe through rail, shipping, energy, and digital networks. A Memorandum of Understanding was signed at the September 2023 G20 summit in New Delhi by India, the U.S., the UAE, Saudi Arabia, France, Germany, Italy, and the European Union. Progress stalled following the outbreak of war in Gaza in October 2023, but renewed momentum emerged in early 2025 with a Trump-Modi joint statement identifying IMEC as a strategic priority and pledging to convene an IMEC partners summit (German Marshall Fund). France had appointed a special IMEC envoy in November 2023, and Italy followed in April 2025 (German Marshall Fund, ECCO). The first collective sherpas meeting was held in France in May 2025, followed by an envoys and sherpas meeting hosted by India in August 2025 (Diplomatist). The EU and India concluded negotiations on a free trade agreement in January 2026, and in March, Italy hosted an IMEC forum in Trieste focused on developing the corridor's Indo-Mediterranean connectivity (ORF, Italian Ministry of Foreign Affairs). 

Despite this diplomatic activity, IMEC still lacks a formal governance structure, an agreed timetable, and dedicated funding, with policy organizations noting that establishing a coordinating body remains an outstanding next step (German Marshall Fund). Multiple policy organizations have recommended establishing a standing coordinating body, with the Atlantic Council urging Washington to leverage U.S. leadership of the 2026 G20 process to create a formal IMEC governance structure (Atlantic Council). However, ongoing India-U.S. trade tensions, unresolved Middle East conflicts, and Saudi Arabia's conditioned stance on Israeli normalization continue to complicate progress toward institutionalization (TRENDS Research).

Resolution Criteria:

This question will be resolved using official government press releases, joint statements, or communiqués from IMEC signatory governments (India, the U.S., UAE, Saudi Arabia, France, Germany, Italy) or the European Commission.

This question will resolve Yes if, by 31 December 2026, a standing coordinating body, secretariat, or formal institutional governance mechanism for IMEC is publicly announced in a joint communiqué, summit declaration, or equivalent document issued on behalf of, or formally endorsed by, a majority of IMEC signatory governments (at least four of the seven national signatories or the European Commission acting on behalf of the EU). The announced body must have an ongoing mandate for coordination, oversight, or implementation of IMEC activities, not merely a mandate for a single event.

The following will NOT be sufficient for resolution:

  • Appointment of individual national special envoys or sherpa-level representatives
  • Ad hoc summits, one-time ministerial meetings, or conference communiqués that do not establish a standing body
  • Proposals or recommendations from think tanks, civil society organizations, or non-signatory governments
  • Informal working groups or sherpa-track meetings without a publicly announced institutional mandate
  • Bilateral coordination mechanisms between two signatories that are not framed as an IMEC-wide governance body
questions.market_info_resolution_criteria: The establishment of a rotating chairmanship for IMEC would resolve the question as “Yes,” provided that it is publicly announced as a formal and ongoing coordination mechanism (e.g., having a clearly defined mandate and regular meetings) and participation is recognized by the signatories. While it would differ from a standing body like a permanent secretariat, a rotating chairmanship would still represent a "formal institutional governance mechanism” for IMEC and thus, would qualify for resolution.

questions.question: Will a bilateral ceasefire or peace agreement in the Russia-Ukraine war take effect by 31 December 2026 and hold for at least 30 consecutive days?
questions.resolution_criteria: Resolves to the outcome of the question found at https://www.randforecastinginitiative.org/questions/1765.
questions.background:
This question asks about whether Russia and Ukraine will agree to and implement a meaningful, bilateral pause in their armed conflict. This includes any qualifying agreement regardless of its intended duration or formal designation, whether described as a ceasefire, armistice, peace agreement, peace treaty, or end of the war.


Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine began on 24 February 2022 and has entered its fifth year, with over 1.5 million estimated total casualties on both sides and ongoing attacks along a roughly 1,200 km front line (Al Jazeera). Since taking office in January 2025, U.S. President Donald Trump has pursued a mediated settlement, delegating negotiations primarily to special envoy Steve Witkoff, senior adviser Jared Kushner, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Ukraine accepted a U.S.-proposed 30-day unconditional ceasefire in March 2025, but Russia has declined to accept a comprehensive truce, insisting that any cessation of hostilities be linked to a full political settlement that addresses its demands on Ukrainian neutrality, military size, and territorial concessions (Wikipedia).

Negotiations have produced several limited or short-term truces rather than a comprehensive ceasefire. These include a partial pause on strikes against energy infrastructure (agreed mid-March 2025), a 32-hour Orthodox Easter truce on 11-12 April 2026 that both sides accused each other of violating within hours (Al Jazeera). Diplomatic activity has continued in parallel: the first trilateral U.S.-Russia-Ukraine meeting since 2022 took place in Abu Dhabi on 23 January 2026, followed by a second Abu Dhabi round on 4 February that produced a 314-person prisoner swap, and Geneva talks on 17-18 February that stalled over Russia's territorial demands (Al Jazeera). Separately, a 'coalition of the willing' led by France and the United Kingdom met in Paris on 6 January 2026 and pledged post-ceasefire security guarantees including potential troop deployments (Al Jazeera). As of mid-April 2026, Security Council Report observers report that U.S.-brokered talks "effectively stalled" in the wake of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, and Russia has continued offensive operations in Donetsk, Kherson, and Sumy regions (Security Council Report).

Resolution Criteria:

This question will resolve "Yes" if a bilateral ceasefire or peace agreement between the internationally recognized governments of Russia and Ukraine takes effect on or before 11:59 p.m. on 31 December 2026 Kyiv time and remains continuously in effect for at least 30 consecutive days. The question will resolve "Yes" on the 30th day after the ceasefire's effective date, once the 30-day continuity threshold has been met. The 30-day period may extend beyond 31 December 2026, provided the ceasefire took effect on or before that date. If a qualifying agreement goes into effect less than 30 days before the scheduled end of the question, the question will remain open until either the ceasefire reaches 30 days (and the question resolves "Yes") or the ceasefire is broken (and the question resolves "No").

The agreement must be formally negotiated and mutually agreed upon by both governments under the same terms, and must apply to the official military forces of both countries. Two separate unilateral declarations, even if they occur simultaneously or mirror each other's actions, do not constitute a bilateral ceasefire for the purpose of this question. A comprehensive peace agreement that ends the war qualifies, as it would inherently include a cessation of hostilities.

The ceasefire or agreement must formally prohibit offensive combat operations (including artillery/missile strikes, ground assaults, aerial bombardment, and naval attacks) across all official and disputed Ukrainian and Russian territory. Continued non-combat military activities (such as resupply, fortification, aerial patrols, or casualty recovery) will not affect resolution. A limited ceasefire (such as one granting safety only to humanitarian corridors or specific regions, or one restricted to a single domain such as strikes on energy infrastructure) is insufficient to resolve the question.

Battlefield violations (such as shelling, drone strikes, or localized assaults) do not, on their own, end the ceasefire for the purpose of this question. The ceasefire will be considered broken if either government formally announces its termination, withdrawal, or that it no longer considers itself bound by the agreement. Without such acknowledgement, the ceasefire will be presumed to remain in effect. If a formal termination or withdrawal occurs before the 30-day mark, the count restarts. The ceasefire would need to be re-established with a new effective date on or before 31 December 2026 and remain continuously in effect for 30 consecutive days from that new effective date for the question to resolve "Yes." If a ceasefire is initially announced for a duration shorter than 30 days but is officially extended without interruption such that the same continuous ceasefire reaches 30 days, the question will resolve "Yes" on the 30th day from the original effective date.

The date the ceasefire goes into effect will be determined using credible international reporting sources and official announcements from Russian and Ukrainian governments, with the Institute for the Study of War's daily Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment (also available on Critical Threats) as a secondary source. The question will be resolved as "No" if a bilateral ceasefire does not enter into effect by 11:59 p.m. on 31 December 2026 Kyiv time or if a qualifying ceasefire does go into effect, but does not hold for 30 consecutive days.

questions.question: Will a U.S. or U.S.-ally satellite be permanently disabled by another country or organization before 1 January 2027?
questions.resolution_criteria: Resolves to the outcome of the question found at https://www.randforecastinginitiative.org/questions/1644.
questions.background:
Space has increasingly become a contested domain as major powers develop sophisticated anti-satellite (ASAT) capabilities targeting both military and civilian satellites. Russia, China, India, and the United States have all demonstrated kinetic ASAT capabilities by destroying their own satellites in tests, while Russia has allegedly begun developing a nuclear space-based anti-satellite weapon that could disable hundreds of satellites in a wide area using through radiation effects or electromagnetic pulse (Wikipedia, CSIS). U.S. Space Force officials have stated that American satellites face daily “reversible” attacks (i.e., attacks that don’t cause permanent damage) from adversaries, including electronic jamming, laser blinding, cyber attacks, and close approaches by other satellites (TWZ). While ASAT systems have not yet been utilized to permanently disable an adversary's satellite, the proliferation of these capabilities and increasing geopolitical tensions have made their potential use more likely.

Resolution Criteria:
This question will be resolved using official statements from the U.S. government (e.g., U.S. Space Force or U.S. Space Command), NATO, or the relevant government agencies of U.S. allies, and/or reporting from open source news agencies. This question will resolve “Yes” if a satellite owned or operated by U.S. or U.S.-ally governments or organizations is confirmed to have been permanently disabled by another country, non-state organization, or entity acting on their behalf.

For the purposes of this question:

  • “Permanently disabled” means that the satellite is rendered inoperable and cannot carry out any of its intended mission. Both kinetic (e.g., collision or physical destruction) and non-kinetic (e.g., cyberattacks) will count. If on 1 January 2027, it is unclear whether an attack has left a satellite permanently disabled, the attack will not be sufficient for resolution. 
  • “U.S. allies” refers to NATO members, countries designated as Major Non-NATO Allies by the United States, and Taiwan.

The following will not be sufficient for resolution:  

  • Satellites disabled during military exercises or testing activities by the satellite’s owner 
  • Technical malfunctions, failing components, or end-of-life decommissioning
  • Temporary disruptions that are later restored
  • Damage that allows the satellite to continue functioning in some capacity
  • Collisions with space debris or other satellites not intentionally directed at the satellite

This question was inspired by a suggestion submitted by RFI user Willard in the RFI Question Lab.
questions.market_info_resolution_criteria: The resolution criteria has been updated to clarify that Taiwan is included in the scope of "U.S. allies" for this question. While Taiwan is not formally designated as a major non-NATO ally by the U.S. State Department, Public Law 107-228 states that Taiwan "shall be treated as" a major non-NATO ally under U.S. law. Consequently, Taiwan-owned or operated satellites will be considered "U.S.-ally satellites" for the purposes of this question.

questions.question: If at least 50,000 people participate in national-level protests in Jordan before 31 December 2026, will those protests escalate into violent internal unrest resulting in at least 50 fatalities across at least three Jordanian governorates?
questions.resolution_criteria: Resolves to the outcome of the question found at https://www.randforecastinginitiative.org/questions/1774.
questions.background:
Jordan has a long history of protest activity but has generally avoided the large-scale violence seen in neighboring countries. During the 2011-2012 Arab Spring, protests spread across multiple governorates, including Amman, Irbid, Ma'an, Karak, and Zarqa, and while there were isolated incidents of violence, including the fatal shooting of one protester in Irbid and the burning of government buildings, the unrest stopped well short of the mass casualty events seen elsewhere in the region (Wikipedia). Jordan's security apparatus, particularly the General Intelligence Department (GID), has historically been effective at containing unrest before it reaches critical levels. The 2018 austerity protests, which brought tens of thousands to the streets nationwide, led to the prime minister's resignation but likewise produced no mass-casualty events (BESA Center).

More recently, pro-Palestine protests since October 2023 have drawn large numbers across the kingdom, with authorities arresting over 1,500 protesters and using tear gas and batons to disperse crowds (Freedom House). In April 2025, Jordan formally outlawed the Muslim Brotherhood, the country's largest opposition movement, after alleging a weapons-manufacturing plot linked to the group, and raided the offices of the Islamic Action Front (IAF), the largest party in parliament, who has been linked to but denies organizational ties to the Brotherhood (Al Jazeera). As of early 2026, the Brotherhood's response has been notably restrained, with no large-scale protests or violent confrontation (Atlantic Council). However, analysts have warned that the ban risks radicalizing members left without a political outlet, particularly amid ongoing regional tensions related to the Gaza war (Stimson Center).

 

Resolution Criteria: 

NOTE: This question is conditional on the 50,000 participant threshold being met. If credible sources do not report national-level protest participation of more than 50,000 people at any point before 31 December 2026, this question will be voided and forecasts will not be scored.

"National-level protests" are defined as demonstrations or protest activity occurring in multiple governorates (at least three of Jordan's twelve governorates) and addressing national political, economic, or social issues, rather than localized or single-issue events. Participation estimates must be supported by credible open sources, including at least one of the following: major international or regional media outlets (e.g., Reuters, Al Jazeera, BBC, Associated Press) citing official or independent estimates; reports from recognized conflict or protest monitoring organizations such as the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED), the International Crisis Group, the Carnegie Endowment, or UN agencies (e.g., the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs); or credible academic or NGO analyses referencing participation data. Participation need not be simultaneous. It may reflect cumulative participation across a clearly connected wave or cycle of national-level protests occurring within a 30-day window.

If the 50,000 participant threshold is met, question will resolve “Yes” if credible open sources document at least 50 fatalities resulting from protest-related violent unrest (including protests, riots, or clashes between protesters and security forces or among civilian groups) across at least three of Jordan's twelve governorates, before 31 December 2026. Fatalities of both civilians and security personnel shall count toward the threshold. Fatalities must be documented by at least two credible, independent open sources, such as major international or regional media outlets (e.g., Reuters, Associated Press, Al Jazeera, BBC), reports from the International Crisis Group, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), Human Rights Watch, or Amnesty International.  

The following will NOT be sufficient for resolution as Yes:

  • Fatalities resulting from terrorism, military operations, or state security actions unrelated to protest activity (e.g., counterterrorism raids, border incidents, or targeted assassinations)
  • Fatalities occurring in only one or two governorates, regardless of total number
  • Protest participation estimates derived solely from social media claims, single partisan sources, or government statements not corroborated by independent reporting

questions.question: Will a Middle Eastern government publicly announce a new agreement permanently stationing Chinese PLA-N naval vessels or personnel on its territory by 31 December 2026?
questions.resolution_criteria: Resolves to the outcome of the question found at https://www.randforecastinginitiative.org/questions/1775.
questions.background:
China operates two confirmed overseas military bases: one established in Djibouti in 2017, and a second at Cambodia's Ream naval base, which the Pentagon's 2025 annual report on Chinese military power formally described as China's second publicly acknowledged overseas military outpost (Newsweek). Chinese navy (i.e., PLA-N) corvettes have been stationed on a rotating basis at Ream since at least December 2023, and in April 2025 China and Cambodia jointly inaugurated a new logistics and training center there, completing a China-funded expansion that included a deep-water pier and dry dock (Stars and Stripes, The Diplomat). Analysts note that visiting third-country vessels have been directed to a separate section of the base from the pier used by Chinese ships, and the extent of any permanent Chinese presence on the northern portion of the base remains unclear (CSIS Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative). The Pentagon's 2025 report assessed that China is seeking to establish additional overseas sites as part of a global logistics and basing network, and listed the United Arab Emirates among countries where China "has likely considered" establishing a basing presence (Newsweek). 

 

Resolution Criteria: 

This question will be resolved using official government statements (from either the host nation or the People's Republic of China) or credible, publicly available reporting on a signed agreement. Relevant official sources include the Chinese Ministry of National Defense and the official government communications portals of Middle Eastern states. Credible secondary reporting from established outlets include (but are not limited to) Reuters, Associated Press, and major regional news organizations.

This question resolves “Yes” if, on or before 31 December 2026, a Middle Eastern government makes a formal public statement, or a verifiable agreement is published, explicitly permitting the permanent stationing of People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLA-N) naval vessels and/or Chinese military naval personnel on its territory. A list of qualifying “Middle Eastern countries” is below:

  • Bahrain
  • Egypt
  • Iran 
  • Iraq
  • Israel
  • Jordan
  • Libya
  • Kuwait
  • Lebanon
  • Oman
  • Qatar
  • Saudi Arabia
  • Syria
  • UAE
  • Yemen

For purposes of this question, “permanent stationing” means an agreement explicitly providing for ongoing or indefinite presence, as distinct from time-limited exercises, temporary port calls, or single-rotation deployments.

The following will NOT be sufficient for resolution:

  • Unilateral U.S. government assessments or intelligence reports alleging Chinese military presence without a corresponding public acknowledgment by the host government or China
  • Port visits, temporary ship calls, or joint naval exercises that do not constitute a formal permanent stationing agreement
  • Reporting based solely on anonymous sources without corroborating official documentation or statements
  • Agreements or arrangements limited to Djibouti or Pakistan, which are explicitly excluded from this question's scope

questions.question: Will Huawei sell or announce plans to sell Open RAN equipment before 1 January 2027?
questions.resolution_criteria: Resolves to the outcome of the question found at https://www.randforecastinginitiative.org/questions/1401.
questions.background:
Open RAN is an effort to push the mobile network industry away from vendor lock-in and towards interoperability, i.e., to allow mobile networks to use equipment from multiple companies instead of having to buy a completely proprietary solution from only one vendor (Network World, Juniper Networks). Huawei, the world’s leading 5G equipment manufacturer, has expressed skepticism towards Open RAN efforts in the past (Light Reading, Strand Consult). In February 2024, Huawei dismissed speculation that plans to support Open RAN were forthcoming (Telecom TV). 

Resolution Criteria: 
This question will be resolved as “Yes” if Huawei sells or announces a commercial Open RAN equipment offering before 1 January 2027. Announcements about research plans or trials of Open RAN equipment will not count.

questions.question: Will another Chinese military base in an African country (excluding Djibouti) be under construction or established by 1 January 2027?
questions.resolution_criteria: Resolves to the outcome of the question found at https://www.randforecastinginitiative.org/questions/1432.
questions.background:
Currently, China’s only military base in Africa is in Djibouti, for which construction was confirmed to begin in February 2016 (The Diplomat). Since the establishment of its military base in Djibouti in 2017, China has shown interest in expanding its military presence in Africa, with significant investments in commercial ports and infrastructure across the continent (USIP, Geopolitical Monitor). 

In recent years, U.S. intelligence reports have indicated that China is considering establishing a military base in Equatorial Guinea, possibly in Bata, which is already home to a Chinese-built deep-water commercial port (Wall Street Journal, U.S. Department of Defense). However, while China has continued to invest heavily in trade and infrastructure projects in the country, plans for such a base have not been confirmed (The Diplomat, Foreign Policy). More recent U.S. government reports have indicated that China may be pursuing a military base in neighboring Gabon (Wall Street Journal, The Diplomat). Other possible locations include Angola, Namibia, Kenya, and Tanzania (Africa Center, The Standard, Modern Diplomacy). 

Resolution Criteria:  
This question will be resolved using open-source news reports and/or official government statements indicating that a groundbreaking ceremony has taken place or that construction has begun on a military facility for use by the People’s Liberation Army in an African country other than Djibouti. 

Additionally, the following scenarios will count towards resolution: 
  • The expansion, conversion, or transfer of an existing port or military facility to allow for use by the People’s Liberation Army, whether for their exclusive use or dual use.
  • Reports that such a facility has been established or is operational, with no previous confirmation of an agreement or construction. 

The following scenarios will NOT count towards resolution:
  • Reports that negotiations are underway or that an agreement has been reached. 
  • Facilities used by Chinese personnel on UN peacekeeping missions will not count towards resolution.
  • Reports that construction is underway on a suspected Chinese overseas military facility will not count unless or until such a facility is confirmed by statements from the Chinese or the relevant African country’s government. 

Additionally, for the purposes of this question:
  • Chinese officials may use the terms “logistical” or “support” facility rather than a “military base”, but any facility constructed for use by the People’s Liberation Army will be considered a military base.
  • An “African country” includes African island nations (e.g., Seychelles, Cabo Verde, Madagascar, etc.).
questions.market_info_resolution_criteria:
For this question to resolve "Yes" based on the conversion of an existing port to dual-use, there must be credible open-source reporting that the port is being operated, managed, or designated for use by the People's Liberation Army, not merely visited by PLA vessels.

Simply docking at a port (such as for a goodwill visit, port call, or resupply stop) would not constitute conversion to a military facility. Even sustained PLA naval presence at a port without official confirmation would be insufficient, as this could represent access rights rather than the establishment of a military facility with basing rights, exclusive zones, or operational control.

questions.question: Will the S&P CoreLogic Case-Shiller Index, a measure of U.S. residential home costs, exceed 350 by July 2027?
questions.resolution_criteria: Resolves to the outcome of the question found at https://www.randforecastinginitiative.org/questions/1645.
questions.background:
The S&P CoreLogic Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index is a widely-followed benchmark that tracks changes in residential real estate prices across the United States (Investopedia). The index uses a repeat-sales methodology, comparing the sales prices of the same properties over time to measure home price appreciation while controlling for differences in home quality and characteristics. The index is calculated monthly and covers all nine U.S. census divisions, with January 2000 serving as the baseline (100) for comparison. At the time of question launch, the most recent Case-Shiller Index for May 2025 was 331.107.

Resolution Criteria:
This question will be resolved using the S&P CoreLogic Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price NSA Index. This question will resolve “Yes” if the Case-Shiller Index is greater than or equal to 350.00000 for any month through July 2027. There is typically a two month lag in reporting, so numbers for July are expected to be available in late September 2027.

Note: There are multiple versions of the Case-Shiller Index, including seasonally adjusted and 20-city or 10-city composite versions. Ensure that you are using data from the Not Seasonally Adjusted S&P CoreLogic Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index (CSUSHPINSA).

questions.question: Before 1 January 2029, will either the U.S. or UK enact a law granting tax incentives to companies that pass an independent security audit for their AI models?
questions.resolution_criteria: Resolves to the outcome of the question found at https://www.randforecastinginitiative.org/questions/1659.
questions.background:
Governments in both the U.S. and UK are increasingly exploring policy mechanisms to incentivize stronger AI security practices among technology companies. The UK published its voluntary Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI in January 2025, which recommends independent security testing and audit trails for AI systems, with the code set to form the basis of a new global standard through the European Telecommunications Standards Institute (Gov.uk). Additionally, the UK government developed a roadmap for trusted third-party AI assurance services after an AI assurance market analysis revealed that third-party assurance providers face significant barriers, including access to information and skills shortages (Gov.uk).  

In the U.S., congressional discussions have highlighted cybersecurity tax credits as a potential tool to encourage secure-by-design principles, with lawmakers like Rep. Michael Guest expressing support for tax incentives for businesses that harden their cybersecurity (Nextgov). However, no AI-specific security audit tax incentive legislation has advanced beyond proposal stages.  

Both countries have strengthened collaboration on AI security guidelines through initiatives like the joint CISA-NCSC secure development guidance, but the transition from voluntary frameworks to mandatory requirements tied to financial incentives would still require legislative action in both countries. 


Resolution Criteria: 

This question will resolve “Yes” if, before 1 January 2029, the U.S. or UK enacts a law that explicitly grants tax incentives to companies conditional upon passing an independent security audit for their AI models. 

In order to qualify for resolution, the law must: 
  • Be formally enacted or signed into law 
  • Explicitly link tax incentives to AI model security audits  
  • Specify that audits must be independent (i.e., conducted by third parties) 
  • Apply to any of a company's AI models

General cybersecurity tax incentives or AI development incentives without specific security audit requirements will not be sufficient for resolution.
questions.market_info_resolution_criteria: To resolve "Yes," the tax incentive must be enacted at the national level by the U.S. federal government or the UK Parliament, not by individual U.S. states, territories, or local jurisdictions.

questions.question: Will Miguel Díaz-Canel cease to hold the position of First Secretary of the Communist Party of Cuba before 1 January 2027?
questions.resolution_criteria: Resolves to the outcome of the question found at https://www.randforecastinginitiative.org/questions/1766.
questions.background:
This question asks about whether Cuba undergoes a leadership transition at the top of its party-state during a period of acute economic crisis, mounting U.S. pressure, and a postponed Party Congress. The First Secretary post is used as the measure because it sits hierarchically above the presidency under Cuba's constitution and is the most direct indicator of who formally leads the Cuban political system.

Miguel Díaz-Canel Bermúdez has served as First Secretary of the Communist Party of Cuba (PCC) since 19 April 2021, when he succeeded Raúl Castro at the close of the 8th Party Congress, becoming the first non-Castro to hold the post since the party's founding (Wikipedia). The First Secretary is the highest office within the PCC and, under Article 5 of Cuba's constitution, the most powerful position in the Cuban party-state, ranking hierarchically above the presidency. PCC congresses are normally held every five years, and the 9th Congress (which would have ratified or replaced the First Secretary) was originally scheduled for 16-19 April 2026 (Granma). On 13 December 2025, the 11th Plenary Session of the Central Committee unanimously approved a postponement of the Congress to an unspecified later date, citing the need to focus on Cuba's economic and energy crisis (Radio Guáimaro).

As of April 2026, Cuba is experiencing nationwide blackouts exceeding 20 hours daily in some provinces, fuel shortages, and a record wave of protests, alongside a U.S. energy blockade imposed by Executive Order 14380 in January 2026 (Cubaheadlines). U.S. President Donald Trump has publicly suggested Cuba could be a target of military action following operations in Venezuela and Iran, and analysts have identified potential institutional successors including Roberto Morales Ojeda (Secretary of Organization of the PCC Central Committee) and Castro-family-linked figures Oscar Pérez-Oliva Fraga and Raúl Guillermo Rodríguez Castro (Al Jazeera). In an interview with NBC News' Meet the Press broadcast on 9 April 2026, Díaz-Canel stated he would not step down, saying "stepping down is not part of our vocabulary" (NPR). Cuba's constitution does not specify a term length for the First Secretary, and the post is filled by election of the Central Committee following a Party Congress.

Resolution Criteria:

This question will resolve "Yes" if, at any point between the date this question opens and 11:59 p.m. Havana time on 31 December 2026, Miguel Díaz-Canel ceases to hold the position of First Secretary of the Communist Party of Cuba for any reason, including but not limited to: replacement at a Party Congress or Central Committee plenary session, voluntary resignation, removal by a party body, death, formal incapacitation resulting in transfer of the title, or abolition of the position. A formal announcement of a future replacement will resolve "Yes" only once the change actually takes effect on or before 31 December 2026; an announcement of a replacement scheduled to occur after that date will not be sufficient. Additionally, if Díaz-Canel is no longer exercising the duties of First Secretary as a result of foreign military action, this question will resolve "Yes" regardless of whether the PCC has formally announced a replacement, provided this is confirmed by major international news outlets (e.g., Reuters, Associated Press, BBC). 

This question will be resolved primarily using official statements from the Communist Party of Cuba published in Granma, the official voice of the PCC Central Committee, and confirmed by reporting from major international news outlets. If sources conflict, Granma will be considered authoritative for the formal status of the position.

The following will NOT be sufficient for resolution as "Yes":

  • Díaz-Canel ceasing to hold other positions (e.g., President of Cuba, Politburo member) while retaining the First Secretary title
  • Reports, speculation, or analyst commentary suggesting Díaz-Canel has lost de facto power, influence, or decision-making authority while formally retaining the title
  • A temporary transfer of duties (e.g., during illness or travel) that does not involve a formal change in titleholder
  • Announcement of a future replacement scheduled to take effect after 31 December 2026

questions.background:
Parliamentary elections are scheduled to be held in Russia in September 2026.

This market will resolve according to the political party that wins the second greatest number of seats in the next Russian State Duma election.

If the results are not known definitively by September 30, 2027, 11:59 PM ET, this market will resolve to "Other".

The named parties or coalitions will be primarily ranked by the number of seats won in the specified election. If two or more parties are tied on seats, ties will be broken by the total number of valid votes received, with higher vote totals ranking higher. If parties remain tied, ties will be broken by alphabetical order of the listed party abbreviations. This market will resolve to the party that occupies the second finishing position after applying this ranking.

This market's resolution will be based solely on the number of seats won by the named party in the State Duma of the Federal Assembly of the Russian Federation.

This market will resolve based on the results of this election as indicated by a consensus of credible reporting. If there is ambiguity, this market will resolve based solely on the official results reported by Russian government sources such as the Central Election Commission of the Russian Federation.

Note: If a listed party contests the election as part of a jointly listed coalition with one or more parties not listed in this market, the market corresponding to the listed party will represent the coalition and will count all seats won by the coalition collectively. questions.resolution_criteria: Resolves to the outcome of the question found at https://polymarket.com/market/will-russia-capture-kostyantynivka-by-september-30-256-333.
questions.background:
This market will resolve to “Yes” if, according to the ISW map, Russia captures the Kostyantynivka railroad station located on Pravoberezhna vulytsia by September 30, 2026 at 11:59 PM ET.

The railroad station will be considered captured if any part of the train station icon is shaded red on the ISW map (https://storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/36a7f6a6f5a9448496de641cf64bd375) by the resolution date. If the area is not shaded red by September 30, 2026, 11:59 PM ET, the market will resolve to “No”.

For any change on the ISW map to qualify for this market’s resolution, the relevant shading indicating Russian control must persist through the next full ISW daily update cycle. If ISW skips a day, shading must persist until the next finalized ISW update is published, regardless of the date. Any continuous shading which reflects either “Assessed Russian Control”, “Assessed Russian Advance In Ukraine”, or “Assessed Russian Gains in the Past 24 Hours” will qualify. “Assessed Russian Infiltration Areas in Ukraine” will not qualify.

If Russia comes into control of this territory as a result of a negotiated settlement, this will qualify for a 'Yes' resolution, regardless of if it is shaded red in the ISW map. An announcement of a negotiated settlement which gives Russia de jure control will not qualify. Actual control must be established.

Once Russia captures the railroad station, any subsequent loss of control will not be considered towards the resolution of this market.

questions.background:

   location;

3. Riots: violent events where demonstrators or mobs of three or more engage in violent or
   destructive acts, including but not limited to physical fights, rock throwing, property
   destruction, etc.;

   are at range and widely destructive;
5. Violence against civilians: violent events where an organized armed group inflicts violence upon
   unarmed non-combatants; and
6. Strategic developments: contextually important information regarding incidents and activities of
   groups that are not recorded as any of the other event types, yet may trigger future events or
   contribute to political dynamics within and across states.

questions.question: Will the option-adjusted spread for the ICE BofA Emerging Markets Corporate Plus Index, which tracks the performance of emerging markets non-sovereign debt within major domestic and Eurobond markets, have increased by {resolution_date} as compared to its value on {forecast_due_date}?
questions.resolution_criteria: Resolves to the value found at https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/BAMLEMCBPIOAS once the data is published.
questions.background:
The notes from the release: N/A.  The notes from the series: Starting in April 2026, this series will only include 3 years of observations. For more data, go to the source.

This data represents the Option-Adjusted Spread (OAS) for the ICE BofA Emerging Markets Corporate Plus Index (https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/BAMLEMCBPITRIV?cid=32413), which tracks the performance of US dollar (USD) and Euro denominated emerging markets non-sovereign debt publicly issued within the major domestic and Eurobond markets. To qualify for inclusion in the index, the issuer of debt must have risk exposure to countries other than members of the FX G10 (US, Japan, New Zealand, Australia, Canada, Sweden, UK, Switzerland, Norway, and Euro Currency Members), all Western European countries, and territories of the US and Western European countries. Each security must also be denominated in USD or Euro with a time to maturity greater than 1 year and have a fixed coupon. For inclusion in the index, investment grade rated bonds of qualifying issuers must have at least 250 million (Euro or USD) in outstanding face value, and below investment grade rated bonds must have at least 100 million (Euro or USD) in outstanding face value. The index includes corporate and quasi-government debt of qualifying countries, but excludes sovereign and supranational debt. Other types of securities acceptable for inclusion in this index are: original issue zero coupon bonds, "global" securities (debt issued in the US domestic bond markets as well the Eurobond Market simultaneously), 144a securities, pay-in-kind securities (includes toggle notes), callable perpetual securities (qualify if they are at least one year from the first call date), fixed-to-floating rate securities (qualify if the securities are callable within the fixed rate period and are at least one year from the last call prior to the date the bond transitions from a fixed to a floating rate security). Defaulted securities are excluded from the Index.
ICE BofA Explains the Construction Methodology of this series as:
Index constituents are capitalization-weighted based on their current amount outstanding. With the exception of US mortgage pass-throughs and US structured products (ABS, CMBS and CMOs), accrued interest is calculated assuming next-day settlement. Accrued interest for US mortgage pass-through and US structured products is calculated assuming same-day settlement. Cash flows from bond payments that are received during the month are retained in the index until
the end of the month and then are removed as part of the rebalancing. Cash does not earn any reinvestment income while it is held in the Index. The Index is rebalanced on the last calendar day of the month, based on information available up to and including the third business day before the last business day of the month. Issues that meet the qualifying criteria are included in the Index for the following month. Issues that no longer meet the criteria during the course of the month remain in the Index until the next month-end rebalancing at which point they are removed from the Index.

The ICE BofA OASs are the calculated spreads between a computed OAS index of all bonds in a given rating category and a spot Treasury curve. An OAS index is constructed using each constituent bond's OAS, weighted by market capitalization. When the last calendar day of the month takes place on the weekend, weekend observations will occur as a result of month ending accrued interest adjustments. When the last calendar day of the month takes place on the weekend, weekend observations will occur as a result of month ending accrued interest adjustments.

questions.resolution_criteria: Resolves to the value found at https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/NFCIRISK once the data is published.
questions.background:
The notes from the release: N/A.  The notes from the series: The Chicago Fed’s National Financial Conditions Index (NFCI) provides a comprehensive weekly update on U.S. financial conditions in money markets, debt and equity markets, and the traditional and “shadow” banking systems. Source: http://www.chicagofed.org/webpages/publications/nfci/index.cfm.

"Positive values of the NFCI indicate financial conditions that are tighter than average, while negative values indicate financial conditions that are looser than average."

"The three subindexes of the NFCI (risk, credit and leverage) allow for a more detailed examination of the movements in the NFCI. Like the NFCI, each is constructed to have an average value of zero and a standard deviation of one over a sample period extending back to 1971. The risk subindex captures volatility and funding risk in the financial sector; the credit subindex is composed of measures of credit conditions; and the leverage subindex consists of debt and equity measures. Increasing risk, tighter credit conditions and declining leverage are consistent with tightening financial conditions. Thus, a positive value for an individual subindex indicates that the corresponding aspect of financial conditions is tighter than on average, while negative values indicate the opposite." Source: http://www.chicagofed.org/webpages/research/data/nfci/background.cfm.

For further information, please visit the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago's NFCI website at http://www.chicagofed.org/webpages/publications/nfci/index.cfm.. A reverse repurchase agreement (known as reverse repo or RRP) is a transaction in which the New York Fed under the authorization and direction of the Federal Open Market Committee sells a security to an eligible counterparty with an agreement to repurchase that same security at a specified price at a specific time in the future. questions.question: Will the term premium on a 10-year zero-coupon bond have increased by {resolution_date} as compared to its value on {forecast_due_date}?
questions.resolution_criteria: Resolves to the value found at https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/THREEFYTP10 once the data is published.
questions.background: The notes from the release: This research reviews a simple three-factor arbitrage-free term structure model estimated by Federal Reserve Board staff and reports results obtained from fitting this model to U.S. Treasury yields since 1990. The model ascribes a large portion of the decline in long-term yields and distant-horizon forward rates since the middle of 2004 to a fall in term premiums. A variant of the model that incorporates inflation data indicates that about two-thirds of the decline in nominal term premiums owes to a fall in real term premiums, but estimated compensation for inflation risk has diminished as well..  The notes from the series: Kim and Wright (2005) produced this data by fitting a simple three-factor arbitrage-free term structure model to U.S. Treasury yields since 1990, in order to evaluate the behavior of long-term yields, distant-horizon forward rates, and term premiums. For the full paper, please go to http://www.federalreserve.gov/pubs/feds/2005/200533/200533abs.html.  Additional background of the series:  1. the units of the series: Percent.  2. the seasonal adjustments of the series:  Not Seasonally Adjusted  3. the update frequency: Daily

questions.question: Will the effective yield of the ICE BofA Euro High Yield Index, which tracks the performance of below investment grade corporate debt issued in the euro domestic or eurobond markets, have increased by {resolution_date} as compared to its value on {forecast_due_date}?
questions.resolution_criteria: Resolves to the value found at https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/BAMLHE00EHYIEY once the data is published.
questions.background:
The notes from the release: N/A.  The notes from the series: Starting in April 2026, this series will only include 3 years of observations. For more data, go to the source.

This data represents the effective yield of the ICE BofA Euro High Yield Index tracks the performance of Euro denominated below investment grade corporate debt publicly issued in the euro domestic or eurobond markets. Qualifying securities must have a below investment grade rating (based on an average of Moody's, S&P, and Fitch). Qualifying securities must have at least one year remaining term to maturity, a fixed coupon schedule, and a minimum amount outstanding of Euro 100 million. Original issue zero coupon bonds, "global" securities (debt issued simultaneously in the eurobond and euro domestic markets), 144a securities and pay-in-kind securities, including toggle notes, qualify for inclusion in the Index. Callable perpetual securities qualify provided they are at least one year from the first call date. Fixed-to-floating rate securities also qualify provided they are callable within the fixed rate period and are at least one year from the last call prior to the date the bond transitions from a fixed to a floating rate security. Defaulted, warrant-bearing and euro legacy currency securities are excluded from the Index.

ICE BofA Explains the Construction Methodology of this series as:
Index constituents are capitalization-weighted based on their current amount outstanding. With the exception of U.S. mortgage pass-throughs and U.S. structured products (ABS, CMBS and CMOs), accrued interest is calculated assuming next-day settlement. Accrued interest for U.S. mortgage pass-through and U.S. structured products is calculated assuming same-day settlement. Cash flows from bond payments that are received during the month are retained in the index until
the end of the month and then are removed as part of the rebalancing. Cash does not earn any reinvestment income while it is held in the Index. The Index is rebalanced on the last calendar day of the month, based on information available up to and including the third business day before the last business day of the month. Issues that meet the qualifying criteria are included in the Index for the following month. Issues that no longer meet the criteria during the course of the month remain in the Index until the next month-end rebalancing at which point they are removed from the Index.

questions.question: Will the US national deposit rate for 12-month certificates of deposit (CDs) have increased by {resolution_date} as compared to its value on {forecast_due_date}?
questions.resolution_criteria: Resolves to the value found at https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/NDR12MCD once the data is published.
questions.background:
The notes from the release: N/A.  The notes from the series: On December 15, 2020, the FDIC Board of Directors approved a Final Rule (https://www.fdic.gov/news/board/2020/2020-12-15-notice-dis-a-fr.pdf) making certain revisions to the interest rate restrictions applicable to less than well capitalized institutions (as defined in Section 38 of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act), which are effective on April 1, 2021. The interest rate restrictions generally limit a less than well capitalized institution from soliciting deposits by offering rates that significantly exceed rates in its prevailing market.

The Final Rule redefined the "national rate" as the average of rates paid by all insured depository institutions and credit unions for which data is available, with rates weighted by each institution's share of domestic deposits. The "national rate cap" is calculated as the higher of: (1) the national rate plus 75 basis points; or (2) 120 percent of the current yield on similar maturity U.S. Treasury obligations plus 75 basis points. The national rate cap for non-maturity deposits is the higher of the national rate plus 75 basis points or the federal funds rate plus 75 basis points.

A less than well capitalized institution may use the "local rate cap" in place of the national rate cap for deposits gathered from within the institution's local market area. The Final Rule redefined the "local rate cap" for a particular deposit product as 90 percent of the highest rate offered on the deposit product by an institution or credit union accepting deposits at a physical location within the institution's local market area.

In accordance with Section 337.7(d), an insured depository institution that seeks to pay a rate of interest up to its local market rate cap shall provide notice and evidence of the highest rate paid on a particular deposit product in the institution's local market areas to the appropriate FDIC regional director. The institution shall update its evidence and calculations for existing and new accounts monthly unless otherwise instructed by the appropriate FDIC regional director, and retain such information available for at least the two most recent examination cycles and, upon the FDIC's request, provide the documentation to the appropriate FDIC regional office and to examination staff during any subsequent examinations..  Additional background of the series:  1. the units of the series: Percent.  2. the seasonal adjustments of the series:  Not Seasonally Adjusted  3. the update frequency: Monthly
